questions.question: What is the main goal of crypto-agility in an engineering system?
options: Make algorithm changes safe and measurable via policy-driven selection and controlled rollout
Support as many algorithms as possible to maximize compatibility
Hide which algorithm is used so attackers cannot target it
Avoid having to rotate keys by using longer key sizes
questions.explanation: Crypto-agility is about safe change over time: explicit policy constraints, deterministic selection, telemetry, and rollback/kill switches.

questions.question: Which pair best captures the difference between capability and policy?
options: Capability is what code can do; policy is what production is allowed to do today
Capability is what attackers can do; policy is what defenders can do
Capability is performance; policy is correctness
Capability is encryption; policy is authentication
questions.explanation: A component may support many algorithms, but policy determines which are permitted in a given environment and time window.

questions.question: In the lesson code, why does `canonicalize_alg_id` exist?
options: To enforce a stable, comparable algorithm ID so different components don't disagree about strings
To make algorithms cryptographically stronger by normalizing names
To compress algorithm IDs for network transport efficiency
To randomly rename algorithms to prevent fingerprinting
questions.explanation: Crypto-agility treats algorithm IDs as an API: canonicalization prevents silent mismatches like "Ed25519" vs "ed_25519".

questions.question: What does a policy allowlist typically mean in negotiation logic?
options: Only algorithms explicitly listed may be selected; everything else is rejected
Algorithms not listed are preferred but not required
Algorithms listed are disabled until a feature flag is turned on
Algorithms listed are automatically considered secure forever
questions.explanation: An allowlist is a constraint: selection must come from that set (plus any other explicit policy rules like version gates and deprecation).

questions.question: Why is an emergency denylist (kill switch) valuable during PQ migration?
options: It lets you rapidly block a broken/deprecated algorithm across deployments without code changes
It improves performance by reducing handshake messages
It prevents key reuse by forcing new randomness
It guarantees forward secrecy even with static keys
questions.explanation: When an algorithm becomes unacceptable, you want one fast control point to disable it everywhere and stop negotiation immediately.

questions.question: A downgrade attack in a negotiable protocol is best described as:
options: An attacker forces peers to select a weaker or unintended but still accepted suite by manipulating negotiation
An attacker breaks the math of a strong algorithm directly
An attacker steals a private key from disk using malware
An attacker tricks a user into reusing a password
questions.explanation: Downgrades target the seams: if negotiation can be influenced into an allowed-but-weak choice, the system becomes weaker without breaking the math.

questions.question: In `negotiate_suite`, why is it important that the chosen suite passes policy for both the signature and KEM?
options: Because the security of the combined handshake depends on both algorithms, and policy must gate every selection path
Because policy only matters for signatures, not for key establishment
Because it makes the negotiation faster by filtering earlier
Because it prevents servers from ever changing preferences
questions.explanation: A suite is a bundle: if either part is disallowed or deprecated, negotiation must reject it to avoid accidental use of unsafe components.

questions.question: What is the most direct reason to log negotiated algorithm IDs (suite IDs) in production?
options: To measure real-world usage and detect regressions or unexpected fallbacks during rollout
To make clients trust the server more by showing internal state
To hide which algorithms are used by mixing logs
To avoid having to document configuration
questions.explanation: Telemetry turns migration into a measurable process: you can see what is actually negotiated and catch surprises early.
